newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM asks parliament to OK leases on US bases.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM asks parliament to OK leases on US bases.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto asked parliament on Thursday to approve a bill to extend leases on land for U.S. military bases.

Hashimoto said he needs the authority to meet a May 14 deadline on expiry of leases on private land used for U.S. military facilities on the southern island of Okinawa, where 75 percent of such installations in Japan are located.
"We have a responsibility to provide bases and facilities for the U.S. military as part of the Japanese government's obligation under the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty," Hashimoto told parliament.
At stake are plots of land owned by 3,000 anti-bases activists who are refusing to renew the contracts. Another 29,000 landowners have agreed to renew their leases.
The contracts in question are mostly for small plots totalling some 36 hectares (89 acres) on which 12 bases, including the U.S. Air Force's huge Kadena Air Base, are located.
The extension of the leases is now before an Okinawan land expropriation committee, which is thought unlikely to reach a decision before the May deadline.
Without revising an existing law on land expropriation, the government would be illegally occupying the land.
The legislation will give the government a temporary extension of its leases after current contracts expire.

Although Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) lacks a majority in parliament, the bill was expected to be passed with the help of small parties and some independent and opposition legislators, parliamentary sources said.

Hashimoto failed to win formal support from the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) on Wednesday night, but many Shinshinto legislators said they would vote for the bill. Deliberations on it will start next Monday.
Government officials have said Hashimoto wants parliament to pass the bill by late April, when he travels to Washington for talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton.

A row between the central and Okinawan governments over U.S. bases flared up in September 1995 when three U.S. servicemen were arrested for the rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl. They are now serving prison terms.
Local authorities on Okinawa, where about half of the 40,000 U.S. military personnel in Japan are stationed, want the bases closed by 2015 but Tokyo strongly opposes such a move.

The concentration of U.S. military facilities on Okinawa is a legacy of the U.S. military occupation of the island between 1945 and 1972. Private land for U.S. bases is expropriated by the Japanese government, not the U.S. military itself.
